name: Dusky Blue
lede: Dusky Blue is a dark, greyed [[blue]] with three separate sources on file, from Ridgway's 1912 plates to the 2010 xkcd survey.

sections.title: Three systems, one dark blue
sections.body:
Robert Ridgway's 1912 color nomenclature, built for naturalists describing birds and eggs, places this color on plate XXII at hue 49, tone "m" for medium; Ridgway's plates are scans of an aged printed swatch book, so the reading is approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS 1955 dictionary separately lists it in block 185, among colors called "pale blue", 5.0 units away in our conversion [2]. The 2010 xkcd survey records the same word again, decades later [3].

In Munsell terms it reads about 6.1PB 2.7/4.1, a dark, fairly desaturated blue leaning toward purple [2]. The xkcd survey's own swatch for the phrase runs slightly more purple than our main value, by a visible but modest margin [3]. The nearest named colors on file are [[colonial]], [[freedom]] and [[flag]], at 2.8, 2.9 and 4 ΔE [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 162 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.7 percent, the most of any color, as photographed [4]. The earliest dated match is Taddeo Gaddi's 1355 *Madonna and Child Enthroned with Angels and Saints*, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [4]. The 1900s rise to nearly five times the archive's overall rate, a sharper jump than the smoother climb across the centuries before it, our clearest surprise in this group [4]. [[painter:henri-matisse|Henri Matisse]] and the Danish painter Vilhelm Lundstrøm both used it heavily, Lundstrøm at close to 43 times the baseline rate [4]. Across its matches it plays a shadow more than two-thirds of the time, almost never a highlight [4]. It keeps company most with [[navy]] and [[slate]] on the same canvases [4]. These counts are computed color matches on photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [4].
